paper_title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.

sections.content: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring Vaishnavi Chaughule, Yuchen Zhang, Mohammed Ahnaf Tajwar, Sai Akshay Menta, Saanidhya Vats, Vinija Jain, Aman Chadha, Divya Chaudhary Khoury College of Computer Sciences, Northeastern University, USA Meta, USA Apple, USA AbstractAgentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made decision. We audit such pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. deterministic walletscore override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and verification gate cancels most of the judges own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLMs justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged transaction. Index Termscryptocurrency, anti-money laundering, illicit transaction monitoring, LLM agents, retrieval-augmented generation, accountability I. INTRODUCTION Cryptocurrency networks carry illicit flows from darknetmarket sales, ransomware payments and laundering through mixers, and exchanges and investigators rely on graph-based detectors to find them [1, 2]. Financial crime compliance is moving from single detection models to pipelines of cooperating agents [3, 4]. These systems are often called explainable because an LLM writes regulation-citing justification for each case [5], but whether that justification is reliable, or reflects the component that decided, is rarely tested. justification is not the same as knowing who decided. When Accepted to the 3rd Workshop on Big Data Analysis AND Illicit Trends (BANDIT) at IEEE BigData 2026. 2026 IEEE. Personal use of this material is permitted. Permission from IEEE must be obtained for all other uses, in any current or future media, including reprinting/republishing this material for advertising or promotional purposes, creating new collective works, for resale or redistribution to servers or lists, or reuse of any copyrighted component of this work in other works. graph model, rule, retriever, verifier, and an LLM judge all touch case, the component that determines the outcome can differ from the component that explains it. This is an accountability problem. An auditor reviewing an escalation needs to attribute it to responsible component, and that attribution has to survive delegation from one agent to the next. End-to-end accuracy cannot provide it: pipeline can score well while its judge has no causal role. Explanationquality ratings cannot provide it either, because fluent justification can be written for decision someone else made. We study this in multi-agent AML pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset [2]. An investigator agent gathers evidence with bounded tool use, compliance agent retrieves regulatory clauses, an LLM judge issues verdict, an entailment gate checks that verdict against the cited clauses, and deterministic wallet-score override can flag case on its own  (Fig. 1)  . We ask three research questions. RQ1: which component decides the outcome of case? RQ2: does the LLM judge decide from the evidence or from the upstream risk score? RQ3: do the answers hold under another pipeline structure, judge backbone, and out-of-sample cases, and do the detectorlevel findings transfer to second dataset? a) Why not an ablation: Removing component and measuring the change in accuracy answers different question. An ablation reports the average effect of components absence. It does not say, for given case, which component was an actual cause of that cases decision. It cannot assign signed credit when one component cancels another, and it cannot separate judge that agrees with an override from judge that copies the overrides input. Decision-source attribution works on individual traces, asks counterfactual questions about each components output, and states which conclusions follow from the design alone. b) Contributions, in order of importance: 1) An audit of an agentic AML pipeline that answers the three questions. RQ1: once truncation failure that made the judge look inert is fixed, wallet-score override still carries about 94% of flag credit. RQ2: on anonymous features the judge follows an injected score across 76 quality with experts. None of these measures which component causes each decision. b) Two published pipelines: We applied the protocols interventions to two published pipelines with public code. OCR-APT [6] detects attacks in provenance graphs with GNN and has an LLM write an attack report for each subgraph the GNN flags. On DARPA TC3 CADETS we passed all 26 candidate subgraphs, 8 malicious and 18 benign, to the LLM, including benign ones the GNN does not flag. It reported every one as an attack, and still called all 26 malicious after we removed the anomaly-alert wording from the prompt and asked for an explicit malicious-or-benign verdict. The GNNs selection is the only decision source; the report describes that decision without discriminating. RiskTagger [7] has an LLM grade laundering suspicion for Ethereum addresses. In its released code every graded level maps to label 1, no suspicion answer drops the address without label, and label 0 comes only from deterministic skip. On 20 addresses attributed to the Bybit hack and 20 presumed-benign addresses, rerunning identical inputs changed the graded level for 21 of 40, injecting upstream high-risk tags changed it for 21 of 40, and the final label changed for at most 1 of 20 in each group. The label comes from the mapping rule, not from the LLMs grading. Both audits used local Llama 8B model rather than the authors models, on small samples. c) Graph-based AML detection: Elliptic [1] and Elliptic++ [2] are the standard Bitcoin benchmarks, and random forests on node features remain strong baselines [1, 8]; relational transformers have also been applied to card fraud [9]. Distance to known illicit nodes carries signal [10], but proximity reflects graph structure rather than behavior, which limits how well it separates licit from illicit activity [11]. d) Attribution in multi-agent LLM systems: The closest line of work is automated failure attribution. Zhang et al. [12] collect failure logs from 127 LLM multi-agent systems, annotate the responsible agent and the decisive step, and find that LLM-based attributors identify the agent in at most 53.5% of cases and the step in 14.2%. Concurrent work uses Shapley-style credit to train or tune agents: Li et al. [13] use it as reward signal, and Xia et al. [14] use it for prompt optimization over workflow graphs; teacher uncertainty has also been used to locate the critical decision steps of multiturn agents for distillation [15]. In addition, Mu and Najib [16] define counterfactual responsibility for probabilistic multiagent systems and relate it to the Shapley value. We differ in three ways. We attribute every decision, including correct ones, not only failures. We compute attribution by intervening on recorded component outputs and re-executing the pipeline, not by asking an LLM to read the log. And we use credit to test whether an evaluation can be trusted, not to optimize the agents. e) Causal responsibility, credit, and mediation: We build on actual causation in the updated HalpernPearl definition [17], which we implement rather than the later modified definition [18], degree of responsibility [19], and the Shapley value [20] in its interventional form [21]. Different Shapley Fig. 1. The audited pipeline. The LLM chain (investigator, compliance agent, judge, gate) produces verdict, but deterministic wallet-score override can flag case on its own (red path), without passing through the judge. The transaction score is shown to the judge and also decides escalation to SAR. evidence bundles and four backbones and cites clauses that do not apply. RQ3: structure matters more than the backbone, and out of sample the pipeline does not separate illicit from licit cases; on AMLworld labelfree proxy override again carries the detection, by thin margin, and the judge again follows the score. 2) Decision-source attribution, protocol with three layers (per-case actual cause and responsibility, interventional Shapley credit, mediation of upstream signals), explicit null policies, matched negative controls with stated falsification conditions, and estimators validated against hand-derived answers. It needs only execution traces and the ability to intervene on component outputs. 3) Structural propositions that identify which attribution results carry no empirical content in given pipeline, so that design consequences are not reported as findings. II. RELATED WORK a) Agentic financial crime compliance: Axelsen et al. [3] design an agentic system covering onboarding, monitoring, investigation, and reporting, evaluated formatively through stakeholder walkthroughs. Naik et al. [4] draft suspicious activity report narratives after activity is already flagged. Khanvilkar and Kommuru [5] combine GNN detector with retrieval-augmented GPT-4 explanations and rate explanation variants can give different answers to the same question [22], which is why we fix null policies before computing credit. Shapley credit has been assigned to components inside network [23], and natural direct and indirect effects [24] have been estimated from observational data [25] and by intervention inside language models [26]. In observational settings the cross-world terms of mediation need identification assumptions; in pipeline that can be re-executed they are computed directly. f) Evaluating compound AI systems: Systems that chain models, retrievers, tools, and rules [27] are mostly evaluated end to end. Kapoor et al. [28] show that accuracy-only agent evaluation has led to mistaken conclusions about where accuracy gains come from, and call for cost-controlled comparisons against simple baselines. Likewise, valid action and correct final answer do not show that an agent knows what its action will do [29]. Our audit is concrete case of the problem they describe: behavior credited to an LLM judge is produced by fixed rule. Decision-source attribution adds per-case, percomponent evidence to end-to-end metrics. g) Validity of LLM judges: anchoring and sycophancy: LLM-as-a-judge is widely used [30], and judges show position bias [31] and range of other biases, including deference to authoritative-looking content [32]. LLMs are anchored by numeric hints, and chain-of-thought, reflection, and instructions to ignore the anchor do not remove the effect [33]. single misleading signal in context flips correct answers across open models, so judges should be assessed on selective trust rather than resistance alone [34]. Even when the evidence provably does or does not determine the answer, models answer largely regardless of which [35], and many errors come from how the input is read rather than from reasoning [36]. Models also tend to agree with views stated in the prompt [37], which parallels automation bias in people who defer to automated aids [38]. Our score-injection and blind-first results fit this picture, and the prompt-level failures reported by Lou and Sun [33] are why we change the pipelines structure rather than its prompt. These studies test judge in isolation and ask whether its verdict is correct. In pipeline, the anchor is often also read by deterministic rule, so biased judge and an override can produce the same decision. We ask prior question, whether the judges verdict causes the systems decision at all, and only attribution separates the two. III. DECISION-SOURCE ATTRIBUTION Decision-source attribution asks, for given case and given decision, which components of pipeline produced it. We treat the pipeline as program that can be re-executed with component outputs replaced, and define three quantities of increasing scope: whether component was source of one decision (Layer 1), how much aggregate credit it earns over its own randomness and its interactions with other components (Layer 2), and how much of an upstream signals effect on the decision passes through it (Layer 3). a) Setting: pipeline maps case to decision D, finite set of dispositions (for example {CLEAR, REVIEW, ESCALATE}, or the four dispositions of the audited pipeline: SAR, RULE GAP, MONITOR and CLEAR). It is composed of components = {c1, . . . , cn}: models, rules, retrievers, LLM judges and gates. Component ci produces an output oi = fi(pai, εi) from the outputs of its parents pai and its own randomness εi (sampling temperature, retrieval ties); deterministic components have no εi. fixed decision function maps the outputs to = g(o1, . . . , on). The trace of case records every oi. An attribution claim is always about an outcome event D, written YA = [d A]: for example flagged, escalated or seen by human. component can be the source of one event and not another, so every claim below names its event. b) Interventions and null policies: For each component we fix in advance null policy νi: the output the rest of the pipeline receives when ci is removed. It must be valid value of cis interface, so the pipeline still runs, and it encodes what the pipeline would do without the component: an LLM judge that is off abstains, verification gate that is off passes its input through, rule that is off never fires. The intervention do(ci=νi) replaces oi with νi and leaves every other mechanism unchanged. Null policies are part of the claim, so we state them with each result and report how sensitive the credit is to the alternatives. c) Layer 1: decision source of single case: Component ci is but-for decision source of event on case if YA(x) = YA (cid:0)x; do(ci=νi)(cid:1), with every other component at the value it took in the trace. When several components could each produce the decision alone, no single one is but-for source, so we use actual causation in the updated HalpernPearl form [17]. contingency {ci}, set to non-actual values w, is valid if (AC2a) some alternative value of ci changes the event under =w, and (AC2b) with ci at its actual value the event keeps its actual value for every subset of set to and every subset of the intermediate variables held at their actual values. The degree of responsibility of ci is 1/(1 + k), where is the size of the smallest valid contingency, and 0 if none exists [19]; but-for is the case = 0. Causes are single components, so minimality holds trivially, and contingencies range over components only, with intermediates entering through the AC2b clause. When the trace does not record components output (our gate result is stored only when it fires), we compute responsibility under every value consistent with the record and report the range. Layer 1 answers the auditors question for one case and one realized trace. d) Layer 2: interventional credit: single trace hides two things: stochastic component may decide differently on rerun, and components interact (a judges flag matters only if gate lets it through). We therefore define, for each case and event, the value of coalition as the probability of the event when the components in run and the others are at their nulls, vx(S) = Eε (cid:104) (cid:0)x; do(cj=νj for / S)(cid:1)(cid:105) , YA and the credit of ci as its interventional Shapley value [21], ϕi(x) = (cid:88) wS (cid:2)vx(S {ci}) vx(S)(cid:3), SC{ci} with wS = S! (n 1)!/n!. The credits add up to vx(C) vx(), the change in the events probability between the full pipeline and the all-null pipeline. Credit is signed: component that moves the decision away from A, such as gate that cancels judges flags, earns negative credit. Group credit is the mean of ϕi(x) over the cases of group. We report credit by group (licit controls, illicit cases, score bands), never only overall, because component can add false alarms in one group and catches in another. e) Layer 3: mediated influence of upstream signals: Layers 1 and 2 say which component decides, not why. When an upstream signal (a detectors risk score) is read both by the judge and by the deterministic policy, part of its effect passes through the judge and part bypasses it. Writing (sR, J(sJ )) for the outcome when the policy reads score sR and the judge reads score sJ , we use the natural direct and indirect effects [24] of moving from to s: NDE = E(cid:2)Y (s, J(s))(cid:3) E(cid:2)Y (s, J(s))(cid:3), NIE = E(cid:2)Y (s, J(s))(cid:3) E(cid:2)Y (s, J(s))(cid:3), with total effect TE = E[Y (s, J(s))] E[Y (s, J(s))]. NIE measures how much the judge follows the score (anchoring); NDE measures how much the rules act on it regardless of the judge. Because the pipeline is program, the cross-world terms are computed directly, by sampling the judge under one score and running the policy under another, so no identification assumptions are needed. With nonlinear decision function, TE need not equal NDE + NIE, so we report all three. f) Estimation: Algorithm 1 gives the estimator. Upstream evidence (the investigation) is gathered once per case and frozen, so every coalition and every score condition is judged on byte-identical evidence; credit is therefore conditional on that investigation. Because the investigator saw the scores, and one of its tools returned label-derived fields in 17 of 154 investigations, ex can itself encode the score and, in those cases, the label; Layers 2 and 3 measure credit given this evidence, not over score-free investigation. Stochastic components are sampled times per case, and components that consume another stochastic output (a gate checking judges citations) are sampled times per upstream sample, which gives an unbiased nested estimate of each vx(S). With small (three or four players), all 2n coalitions are evaluated exactly. Confidence intervals come from hierarchical bootstrap that resamples cases and, within each case, the stochastic samples. g) When attribution is deductive, and when it is not: Some attribution results follow from the pipelines design and one observed fact, and carry no further information. Attribution becomes an empirical question when (i) components are stochastic, so components contribution depends on how often it acts; (ii) the decision function is non-monotone, so component can push decisions in either direction and its signed credit cannot be read off the design; (iii) components interact, for example when escalation requires both supported judge flag and firing rule, so credit depends on their joint behavior; or (iv) an upstream signal reaches the decision by several paths. These are exactly the cases the three layers are built for, and our worked examples cover each: (i) the full-prompt Layer 2 run, (ii) two-sided override, (iii) the blind-first structure, and (iv) Layer 3. h) Structural properties: Some properties follow from pipelines structure for any data. We state them as propositions before reporting numbers, so that they are not mistaken for findings, and the attribution computation checks each one on every case. Proposition 1 (null judge). Three controls hold by construction (marked S): they check the implementation, not the data, and we report them only as such. j) Validation on synthetic pipelines: Every estimator is tested against answers derived by hand, in exact fractions, before it is applied to the pipeline. For Layer 1, the engine recovers the textbook cases: in disjunctive overdetermination each sufficient cause has responsibility 1/2; in an 110 vote each voter has 1/6; an unread variable has 0; and on nonmonotone gate model it matches hand-derived contingencies where reading without the AC2b clause gives the wrong answer. For Layer 2, the Shapley engine reproduces closed forms for conjunctive, disjunctive and signed gateoverride games, and the sampled and nested estimators are unbiased. For Layer 3, the estimator recovers direct-only, indirect-only and interacting pipelines (where TE = NDE + NIE). IV. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP a) Pipeline: The pipeline is fully local (Figure 1). temporal transaction detector (Balanced-BiEGCN [39]) scores each transaction, and wallet-level graph model (WalletGAT) scores the wallets linked to it. WalletGAT is two-layer GATv2 network (64 hidden units, 4 attention heads in the first layer) over the Elliptic++ wallet graph (822,942 wallets, 5.7M wallet-to-wallet edges, 169 time-aggregated features per wallet), trained with class-weighted cross-entropy and neighbor sampling; 5-seed ensemble reaches test AUC-ROC 0.70 and illicit-class F1 0.28. It is trained on temporal split of the labelled wallets (last activity at timesteps 134 for training, 3541 for validation and 4249 for test), and none of the 37,820 transactions at timesteps 3542 links directly to training wallet. ReAct investigator gathers transaction and neighborhood evidence with bounded tool budget. compliance agent retrieves regulatory clauses from corpus of six regulatory documents with hybrid FAISS and BM25 retrieval and cross-encoder reranking; citations that cannot be matched to retrieved text are stripped, and the agent may abstain. An LLM judge (Llama 3.1 8B unless stated) issues verdict, and an entailment gate downgrades flag when the cited clauses do not support it. deterministic walletscore override then upgrades the verdict to flag when linked wallet scores at least 0.90, rule anchored to FATF Recommendation 20. Escalation to suspicious activity report additionally requires transaction score of at least 0.70. b) Pipeline structures: The current structure is the one above. The blind-first structure hides every score and labelleaking field from the judges prompt, runs the wallet rule separately, and routes cases where the judge and the rule disagree, or where the gate does not support flag, to human review instead of resolving them automatically. c) Evaluation set: All attribution runs use the same 120 cases: 40 wallet-linked hard cases and 80 licit controls (40 HIGH licit and 40 LOW licit by transaction score). The hard cases count as illicit under the wallet-linked label, but at the transaction level 8 are illicit and 32 are licit, so we report the 8 transaction-illicit cases separately. Throughout, hard case means wallet-linked hard case, and illicit without qualification means illicit at the transaction level. The wallet-linked label is not independent of the transaction label: Elliptic++ labels wallet illicit if it takes part in any illicit transaction [2], so for an illicit transaction the hard-case condition holds by construction. The 80 licit controls are transaction-licit, scored transactions before the timestep-43 shift, drawn 40 per band at transaction-score cut of 0.5 with fixed seed. Because WalletGATs training window overlaps them, we also drew 80 out-of-sample controls by the same rule, restricted to timesteps 3542 and to transactions with no wallet within two walletgraph hops (WalletGATs receptive field) active at timesteps 134. d) Datasets: Elliptic++ [2]: 203K Bitcoin transactions and 822K wallets over 49 timesteps, with illicit, licit and unknown labels on anonymous features. It is the main testbed for every layer. IBM AMLworld HI-Small [40]: synthetic bank transfers with ground-truth laundering labels from simulator that plants known typologies (fan-in, fan-out, cycles, scatter-gather and others). Unlike Elliptic++, it has real amounts, currencies and payment formats, and laundering is rare: 956 of 862,792 transfers (0.11%) on the test days. We use it to test whether the findings transfer beyond Bitcoin; we report flags only and do not run the three attribution layers on it. First, there is no trained wallet model for AMLworld, and training one on the same labels would make the override circular, so the override reads label-free proxy: for each account, the highest detector score among its other transfers on the test days, with the transaction under investigation left out. V. RESULTS Each result is tagged as main finding, design consequence (it follows from the design or the layer definitions, not from model behavior) or transfer test. a) Detection baselines: Table II shows that the graph detector is not the strongest model by F1 on either dataset. On AMLworld the detectors are weak in absolute terms at this imbalance and each wins on one metric, so we report both. A. RQ1: Which component decides? a) silent failure: context truncation [main finding]: The initial runs never set the judges context length, so the server silently truncated prompts that exceeded the window it chose. In the Layer 2 rerun on the same 120 cases, the judge returned verdict in all 120 with 32k context, and no verdict in 70% with 4k context. In the original runs the judge never flagged hard case, so by Proposition 1 the override received all the credit by construction. That is consequence of the truncation and the design, and we do not report it as finding about the judge. controlled version on the judge alone separates the two failures. With the context capped at 2,048 tokens, which truncates the system prompt, Llama 3.1 8B and Qwen2.5 14B each returned no valid verdict in any of 720 calls on 24 held-out Elliptic++ transactions, whatever score was shown. At 8,192 tokens it copied the score (Table IV), and with the score line removed it flagged 89% of Group Override Judge Gate +0.554 +0.119 0.087 All 120 Licit controls (80) +0.444 +0.179 0.130 +0.775 Hard cases (40) TABLE III LAYER 2 INTERVENTIONAL SHAPLEY CREDIT FOR THE EVENT FLAGGED, CURRENT STRUCTURE, LLAMA 3.1 8B, 32K CONTEXT. CREDITS SUM TO THE CHANGE IN FLAG PROBABILITY FROM THE ALL-NULL PIPELINE. 0 0 illicit and 87% of licit transactions (Qwen2.5 14B: 33% and 30%). Truncation, visible score and hidden score thus give three different failures, and in none of them does the evidence decide. b) With the full prompt, the override still carries the flags [main finding]: Table III gives Layer 2 credit for the event flagged with the full 32k prompt. The pipeline flags case with probability 0.587 on average. The wallet override earns +0.554, about 94% of that total. The judge earns +0.119, but only on licit controls, where every flag is false alarm, and the gate earns 0.087 because it cancels most of those flags. On the 40 hard cases the override takes all the credit (0.775) and the judge and gate take exactly 0, because the judge never flags hard case; since the wallet rule fires on only 4 of the 8 transaction-illicit cases, most of that credit is for flagging transactions that are licit at the transaction level. The judge therefore acts once it sees its full prompt, but its actions are false alarms that the gate removes. Over all 120 cases the intervals are [0.47, 0.64] for the override, [0.09, 0.15] for the judge and [0.12, 0.06] for the gate (95%, cases resampled; resampling the LLM samples as well changes them by at most 0.001). With the prompt truncated to 4k tokens the override still carries the flags (+0.497, [0.42, 0.57]), but the judges credit is indistinguishable from zero (0.012, [0.047, 0.028]) and the gates turns positive (+0.095, [0.050, 0.137]), so truncation changes which component appears to act, not only how often. Layer 1 gives the same picture on the 160 stored traces of the original runs: for the flag outcome the override is but-for cause in 159 of 160, and on the 70 flagged cases it is but-for cause in all 70 while the judge is one in at most 6. c) The gate decides on clause composition [main finding]: On the 160 real-pipeline assessments of the disagreement sample, the entailment gate fired on 2/160 cases (1.25%, 95% CI [0.34%, 4.44%]). That rate comes from the original runs, where truncation left the judge with few flags to check; with the full prompt the gate cancels most of the judges flags (Table III). The gate prompt contains no behavioral features, and all 20 forced-conflict cases shared one evidence bundle, so we read this as the gate responding to which clauses were retrieved, not to the activity it never sees. Citation verification behaves as designed: 37 of 160 assessments (23.1%) had at least one ungrounded citation stripped, and all 202 surviving citations matched retrieved text. d) non-monotone override: the layers disagree on preemption [design consequence]: To test attribution where the answer cannot be read off the design, we replace the one-sided override by two-sided one: it still raises clear verdict to flag when linked wallet scores at least 0.90, and it now clears flag that passed the gate when every linked wallet scores below τ = 0.50, the wallet models own decision threshold. The variant is evaluated counterfactually on the stored judge and gate samples of both backbones, which is valid because neither model sees the rule; at τ = 0 it reproduces the Layer 2 results exactly. The threshold was first set to 0.10 and moved to 0.50 before any credit was computed, once the wallet scores showed that at 0.10 no case the judge flags could be affected; 0.05, 0.10 and 0.20 are reported as sensitivity. The downgrade changes the outcome on one case (Llama; flag probability 0.20 to 0) and on none for Qwen. Yet it earns Shapley credit of 1/6 on eight casebackbone pairs where the gate already rejects every flag, because Shapley averages over coalitions in which the gate is switched off and the downgrade does the clearing. On the same cases, actual causation gives the downgrade zero responsibility, since in the realized trace the gate fired first and preempted it, and halves the gates responsibility (from 1 to 1/2). Both answers are correct for their question: Layer 2 measures what component contributes across configurations, Layer 1 what it did in this trace. The disagreement is why we report both. B. RQ2: Evidence or score? a) The judge follows the score, not the evidence [main finding]: We tested score injection on the judge alone, with the gate and the override off, over 76 distinct evidence bundles in three cohorts: 24 known-answer cases on synthetic policy; 28 matched violating and compliant cases over 14 AML typologies, identical except for their decisive facts and citing verbatim FATF, EU and FinCEN clauses; and 24 held-out Elliptic++ transactions from timestep 42 with their pipeline clauses. Each case was judged at injected scores 0.10 and 0.90 on byte-identical evidence, by four backbones, under the pipelines prompt, which tells the judge to match its verdict to score-derived risk tier, and under neutral prompt that calls the score an uncertain estimate. Table IV gives the score effect, the share of paired verdicts that flip when only the score changes. The deployed configuration, Llama 3.1 8B with the pipeline prompt, follows the score on nearly every case in every cohort. Scale and prompt help only where the evidence is readable: on the typology cases, Llama 3.1 70Bs effect falls to +15%, and the neutral prompt brings every backbone except Llama 8B to +510%. On the real Elliptic++ transactions all four backbones follow the score on every pair under the pipeline prompt, and Llama 70B does so under the neutral prompt too. On the typology forced-conflict arms, where the evidence is correct by construction (a violating case shown 0.10, compliant one shown 0.90), the deployed configuration follows the wrong score in 96% of calls, against 16% for Llama 70B and 42% for Qwen 14B. The judge can decide from readable evidence, but on the anonymous features the pipeline gives it, the score decides. Deferring to detector with AUC-ROC 0.87 is not irrational when the features are Synth. Typology Elliptic++

With the score hidden, the deployed configuration still flags 90% of violating cases under inapplicable clauses (100% with the matched ones), and Llama 3.1 70B flags 97100% under either prompt; only Qwen2.5 14B with the neutral prompt reads the clauses (99% to 41%, with compliant cases near 0%). substantial share of flags under inapplicable clauses quote one of them verbatim as the basis (Llama 8B 50 of 123, Llama 70B 103 of 138, Qwen 14B 87 of 98), and every such quote passes the pipelines substring check. verified citation shows that the text exists, not that it applies, just as grounding an answer to its location in document [41] shows where it came from, not that it is correct; scale does not make the judge check. c) Layer 3: the judge copies the score, and the pipeline absorbs it [main finding]: We swept the score shown to the judge over 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7 and 0.9 and hidden condition on all 120 cases, with the evidence frozen and = 5 judge samples per level, and crossed it with the score the rules read. Llamas verdict is step function of the score: it flags no sample at 0.1 or 0.3, 15% at 0.5, and every sample at 0.7, at 0.9 and when the score is hidden. Qwen rises more gradually (0%, 0%, 16%, 45% and 62%; 58% hidden). Yet the final flag moves by only 0.037 [0.013, 0.063] for Llama and by exactly 0 for Qwen: the gate rejects almost every judge flag (it passed 32 of 600 for Llama and none for Qwen), and the wallet override decides the rest. By Proposition 3 the flag has no direct path, so this small effect is entirely indirect. For escalation to SAR the score acts mainly through the rules 0.70 cut: the direct effect is 0.32 [0.25, 0.39] for Llama and 0.55 [0.46, 0.64] for Qwen, the indirect effect is zero by construction, and the interaction (+0.09 and 0.07) enters through which clauses the judge cites, not through its verdict. In the blind-first sanity cell, where nothing reads the score, the indirect effect is 0, and 600 of 600 judge replies are byte-identical across the two injected scores. The judge copies the score, but the gate and the override, not the judge, carry it to the decision.

sections.content: H/L licit tx-illicit Seen by human licit (80) tx-illicit (8) Llama, current Qwen, current Llama, blind Qwen, blind 86 / 0 57 / 0 100 / 100 72 / 37 0 0 100 50 57 100 73 35 45 100 100 TABLE BACKBONE STRUCTURE ON 120 CASES (PERCENT OF SAMPLES). SEEN BY HUMAN IS ESCALATE OR REVIEW; ON LICIT CONTROLS EVERY SUCH CASE IS FALSE ALARM. H/L: HIGH LICIT / LOW LICIT. C. RQ3: Do the answers hold? a) Structure matters more than the model [main finding]: Table reports the 22 on the same frozen evidence. In the current structure the two backbones behave alike. With the score visible, Llama flags 86% of HIGH licit samples and 0% of LOW licit ones; Qwen flags 57% and 0%. Both answer no clear violation in all samples on the 8 transaction-illicit cases, so only the 4 of those on which the wallet rule fires can reach human. In the blind-first structure Llama flags every case, which shows that its earlier verdicts were reading the score. Qwen flags 72% of HIGH licit, 37% of LOW licit and 75% of transaction-illicit samples, clears 42% of LOW licit controls, and sends all 8 transaction-illicit cases to human. That is weaker evidence of judgment than it looks. Qwen flags HIGH licit more than LOW licit cases although both are licit and the score is hidden. The blind evidence still predicts HIGH versus LOW band with out-of-fold AUC 0.80 against permuted 0.49 (p = 0.001), because the investigator that gathered it saw the score: its strongest shape features are the number of wallet lookups, tool errors, and whether it hit the step limit. Retrieval was also tiered by score: on the typology cases its queries recover 14% of the case-specific clauses, against 52% for queries built from the case facts, and return the same clauses for violating case and its control. On hard cases Qwen flags transaction-illicit cases only slightly more than transaction-licit ones (75% vs. 62%, = 8, not significant). Changing the structure changes outcomes lot for both models; changing the model matters little in the current structure and lot in blind-first. By Proposition 2, the judge and the wallet rule share escalation credit equally in blindfirst, and the gates credit for seen by human is zero, so we do not report those numbers as findings. b) Out of sample, the pipeline does not separate illicit from licit cases [main finding]: To measure discrimination, we built an out-of-sample hard set: transactions at timesteps 3542 that the detector clears (score < 0.5), under the out-ofsample wallet restriction above, crossed by transaction label and by whether WalletGAT scores any linked wallet at 0.5 or above (26 illicit and 48 licit cases; the 6 illicit cases WalletGAT misses are all included). With the full 32k prompt the pipeline flags 12 of 26 illicit (46.2%) and 18 of 48 licit (37.5%) cases, LR+ 1.23 (95% CI 0.712.14); with the context truncated to 4k, 10/26 and 18/48 (LR+ 1.03). Every flag comes from the wallet override; the judge flags none of the 74 on its own, and no override threshold between 0.50 and 0.99 gives LR+ above 1.2. On the 80 out-of-sample licit controls the pipeline flags 37 (46.3%, 35.757.1%), against 39 of 80 (48.8%) in sample, so the false alarms are not an artifact of WalletGATs training overlap; 36 of the 37 come from the override. Neither the controller nor the score changes this. With the LLM the 32k controller replaced by the fixed safeguard policy, result is identical (12/26, 18/48). Hiding the score from the judge leaves it unchanged (12/26, 19/48, LR+ 1.17), but only because the gate cancels 70 of the judges 74 flags. The signal is in the graph: logistic combiner over ten label-free graph features, trained on timesteps 134, reaches LR+ 3.19 (2.34 4.36; 38.3% recall at 12.0% false-positive rate) on all 81 illicit and 1,352 licit out-of-sample hard cases, against 1.80 for the single-wallet 0.90 rule; it is proof of concept with 56 illicit training cases. c) AMLworld: detectors, override and judge [transfer test]: first run returned no verdict because the clusters HTTP proxy intercepted calls to the local model server; with that fixed, the judge returned verdict in all 120 assessments. On 20 hard laundering cases, all scoring below 0.5, the pipeline flags 7 (35%, 95% CI 1857%), 6 of them through the proxy override, against 1 of 40 licit transfers below 0.5 (2.5%, 0.413%; Fisher = 0.001), also through the override. The margin is thin, because the proxy scores bunch between 0.76 and 0.79. The judge alone flags 1 of the 20 laundering cases, and 3 of 20 when it sees only the transaction. On licit transfers it follows the score band, as on Elliptic++: on its own it flags 13 of 40 above 0.5 and none of 40 below (p < 0.001). The override again carries the detection, and the judge adds false alarms on high-score cases. VI. DISCUSSION a) Explanation is not attribution: This pipeline produces regulation-citing justifications with verified citations while single rule carries most of the decision credit. An evaluation that rated explanation quality, as in prior AML systems, would score it well. The two published pipelines we audited (Section II) show the same pattern: GNNs selection in OCRAPT and label-mapping rule in RiskTagger decide, while the LLM writes. Reasoning traces likewise often omit the injected bias that changed an answer [42]. b) Accountability across delegation: In agent pipelines the agent that speaks last is often not the agent that decided. Attribution exposes form of evaluation gaming that needs no intent: judge that copies an upstream score passes end-to-end checks while contributing nothing, and hiding the score does not remove the copy if an upstream agent that saw it shaped the evidence. Verification therefore has to follow information through the whole delegation chain. c) Design implication: Blind-first reconciliation makes the judges contribution measurable, but it is only as blind as its evidence, and it trades the current structures escalation of high-score licit controls for much larger review load. d) Limitations: We study one pipeline in depth; the two published pipelines received only targeted interventions. Elliptic++ is real but anonymous, and AMLworld is synthetic, uses proxy override, excludes the simulation tail, and is evaluated on flags from one sample per case, without the three attribution layers; its typologies are planted by the same simulator that labels them. The attribution set has only 8 transaction-illicit hard cases and the out-of-sample set 26; larger transaction-illicit sample, ideally the full Elliptic++ test set, with every attribution metric stratified by transaction label, is future work. Several diagnostics use 20 cases, and = 5, = 2 give wide per-case intervals. Attribution is conditional on frozen evidence gathered by Llama controller that saw the scores. One investigator tool returned label-derived fields, including the queried wallets own label, which for an illicit transaction exposes its own label; it was reached in 17 of 154 investigations, and rerunning those without the fields left every licit case unchanged and changed one illicit case, through the override, which never reads those fields. Model family and size change together in the 22, and replies are not seedreproducible across server processes. The two-sided override is counterfactual variant evaluated on stored samples, not deployed rule, and its threshold was re-set once before results were computed. In Layer 3, two Qwen levels were resumed after cluster node killed their jobs, so their samples come from two server processes. The typology cases were written by the authors and reviewed within the team, not adjudicated by compliance officers, and several violating cases paraphrase their clauses, so they test unambiguous evidence rather than legal reasoning.

sections.title: ETHICAL STATEMENT
sections.content: Decision-source attribution can help auditors find which component of an automated system made decision; it could also be used to make rule-driven system appear judgmentdriven, one reason we report structural results separately. All data are public (Elliptic++) or synthetic (AMLworld), and the pipelines outputs should not be used for enforcement without human review.
